title: He Co-Signed To Be Nice. The Debt Became His.

beats.text: Dave's phone rings. A debt collector, about a car he's never driven.
Six months earlier, he signed one piece of paper. For his buddy Bob.
Bob needed a car for a new job. Bad credit. So Dave co-signed an eighteen thousand dollar loan.
A co-signer isn't a reference. It's a second borrower. Same debt. All eighteen thousand dollars.
Three months later, Dave applies for his own mortgage. The loan officer frowns: whose four hundred dollar payment is this?
It's Bob's car. But now it's Dave's debt too.
Then Bob loses that job. And stops paying.
The debt collector calls Dave directly. The lender doesn't even have to chase Bob first.
One signature gave the lender two wallets. For one car.
Dave pays twelve hundred dollars, just to stop it. For a car he's never driven.
Then the letter arrives. Repossession. If the sale doesn't cover the loan, Dave covers the gap.
Owe fifteen thousand. Sells for eight. Dave could owe seven thousand more. For a car that's gone.
So Dave and Bob make a plan. Bob sells it himself, before the deadline, and covers what's left.
The loan closes. Damage stops at twelve hundred. The seven thousand dollar gap never happens.
That night, Dave finds the paper he signed. One sentence was already on it.
If the borrower doesn't pay, you will have to. It had predicted everything.
So here's the rule. Before you co-sign anything, ask: could I pay this whole loan, alone?
If the answer's no, find another way to help your friend.
Subscribe. It's the only paper we'll ever ask you to sign.
